title: Why India is probing cheap aluminium imports for windows and solar stands
subtitle: The DGTR opened an anti-dumping investigation on 9 November into aluminium extrusions shipped by China, Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand.
content_html:
Look at the window in your room. If it has a thin silver frame, that frame may be aluminium, pushed into shape like toothpaste out of a tube. On Monday, 9 November 2026, India's trade watchdog opened an investigation into these aluminium shapes when they come in by ship out of China, Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand. The question it wants to answer is simple: are these goods being sold in India at unfairly low prices?

The watchdog is the Directorate General of Trade Remedies, or DGTR, a body under the commerce ministry. Its notification dated 9 November says the four countries together sent about 90% of all such imports into India during the period it will study.

First, what is an aluminium extrusion?

Think of a sev maker at a namkeen shop. Dough goes into a press with a shaped plate, and long strings come out in that exact shape. Aluminium extrusion works the same way. A solid aluminium block, known as a billet, is heated until it turns soft. Then a strong hydraulic ram pushes it through a steel plate with a shaped hole, called a die. Out comes a long bar with that shape, which is cooled, stretched, cut and hardened in an oven, as the DGTR notification describes.

These long shapes are called profiles. The DGTR's list of what the probe covers is long: doors, windows, railings, heat sinks, lighting profiles, solar mounting structures, ladders and bicycle parts, along with plain bars, rods, tubes and pipes. Kitchen and wardrobe fittings are on the list too.

This video shows how an aluminium bar is pushed through a die to become a profile.

What does "dumping" mean?

Imagine a samosa seller in the next town who sells samosas there for Rs 15 each. Then he comes to your street and sells the same samosa for Rs 8. The samosa stall on your street cannot match that price and starts losing customers. Selling abroad for less than the normal price back home is what trade rules call dumping.

An anti-dumping duty is an extra entry fee charged on such imported goods when they reach the border. The idea is to bring the price back to a fair level, so local makers get a level pitch to play on, like in a fair cricket match.

The DGTR does not charge the duty itself. At the end of a probe, it recommends to the Central Government whether a duty is needed, and how much would be enough to undo the damage.

Who complained, and what do they say?

The push came out of ALEMAI, a group of aluminium extrusion makers. As per the Economic Times report, this group speaks for 228 manufacturers in India. Most of these are small and medium businesses, the DGTR notes.

Their main points, as the DGTR lists them:

  • Imports out of the four countries rose a lot.
  • The imported goods were priced below Indian makers' prices.
  • Indian makers' profits fell, and they are making losses.
  • Their factories are running well below full capacity.

Nine member companies also asked for a duty in their own names. On 4 November, three of them sent their cost numbers to the DGTR, as per Business Standard.

Officially, the DGTR started this case on its own, which is called "suo motu" in legal words. It used the group's papers and the government's own import data to decide there was enough reason to look closer. Its first look found that the gap between the normal price and the export price appears to be more than tiny.

Why are Indian factories half idle?

This complaint did not start this month. In August 2025, the group's leaders told Deccan Herald that India could make 3.5 million tonnes of extrusions a year, but was making only around 2 million tonnes. The remaining 1.5 million tonnes came in as imports.

ALEMAI's president Jitendra Chopra told the paper: "The biggest challenge is the under-utilisation of domestic manufacturing capacity due to cheap imports."

The group also told Deccan Herald that Chinese makers were sending goods into India through Vietnam and Malaysia, using India's free trade deals to pay zero duty. A free trade deal is a promise between countries to cut or drop import taxes on each other's goods. The group asked the government to look again at India's trade deals with the ASEAN countries and the UAE.

What period will the DGTR check?

The probe will study 15 months, 1 April 2025 to 30 June 2026. Usually such a period is 12 months. The DGTR picked a longer one because most of these makers are small firms that keep their books by financial year, from April to March, as the notification explains. To see the harm over time, it will also look back at the years starting 1 April 2022.

There is one more detail. India already charges an anti-dumping duty on anodised aluminium solar panel frames made in China. It came in on 27 September 2024. The DGTR says it will decide during the probe how those frames fit into this new case.

What happens next?

Everyone with a stake, like foreign sellers, Indian importers and users, now gets 37 days to send their answers and data through the DGTR's online portal, called SETU, as Business Standard reports. They have 15 days to comment on which products should be in the list. The DGTR will also pick a sample of Indian makers to work out the fair price and the harm.

Only after all this will the DGTR say whether a duty is needed. Nothing changes at the border today. If a duty does come later, it is paid on the imported pieces, so anyone who buys these imported shapes, like window fitters, furniture makers or solar firms, would pay that extra fee on them. Indian makers, on the other side, would compete on a fairer price.

This video explains how anti-dumping duty works in India.

Why it matters to you

Aluminium shapes are everywhere: in new flats, office buildings, rooftop solar stands and even the ladder in your house. Trade cases like this one decide two things together. One is whether small factories in India can keep running. The other is how much builders and solar firms pay for their parts. For anyone thinking of starting a small trading or making business, this case is a good real lesson in how a price war across borders turns into a government probe.
